Technical details of prespecified endpoint horizons

Graeme L. Hickey

Source: vignettes/endpoint-horizons-technical.Rmd
endpoint-horizons-technical.Rmd

The endpoint-horizon functions allow the endpoint time to change according to a prespecified schedule, conditional on the trial reaching each interim look. The success calculation uses the endpoint assigned to that look. The futility calculation predicts success at the eventual maximum-sample-size endpoint. When these endpoints differ, their predictive models use separate follow-up data cuts.

This vignette describes the statistical calculations and their implementation in sim_horizon_trials(), sim_horizon_paths(), and apply_horizon_rules(). Extending an endpoint from 12 to 18 months provides a worked example. The technical details of the Goldilocks design cover the underlying fixed-horizon methods.

Design specification

Let the interim enrollment sizes be n_1 < \cdots < n_L < N_{\max}, with success endpoint times H_1 \le \cdots \le H_L \le H_F. Here, H_F is the endpoint for the maximum-N final analysis and for every futility prediction. All participants have planned outcome collection through H_F from enrollment, including participants recruited before the endpoint changes. final_horizon therefore specifies both the eventual endpoint and collection duration; no separate collection-horizon argument is needed.

Quantity R argument Interpretation
n_\ell, H_\ell endpoint_schedule Data frame with columns N and horizon; one row per interim
N_{\max} N_total Maximum enrollment; not an additional interim look
H_F final_horizon Maximum-N endpoint, futility prediction horizon, and planned collection duration
Dropout reference time dropout_horizon Time at which prop_loss specifies the dropout probability

The schedule is applied before evaluating each reached look. It does not use an interim estimate or predictive probability to choose whether to extend the endpoint. A terminal stopping decision prevents later scheduled changes from taking effect. If the trial continues to maximum enrollment, its final analysis uses H_F after endpoint ascertainment; reaching N_{\max} does not itself trigger an interim analysis.

An expected-success stop fixes the cohort and its endpoint. If accrual stops at N=300 using a 12-month endpoint, the subsequent final analysis uses those 300 participants at 12 months. If that analysis fails, the trial remains unsuccessful; it does not resume enrollment or switch to an 18-month analysis to establish success. Planned collection through 18 months does not change this rule. Expected success is a reason to stop accrual, not a declaration of final success.

Two data cuts at the same calendar date

Let E_i be enrollment time, T_i the event time from enrollment, and D_i the independent dropout time. The calendar date of look \ell is t_\ell = E_{n_\ell}. For an enrolled participant and an analysis horizon H, the available data are

X_{i\ell}(H) = \min\{T_i, D_i, H, t_\ell-E_i\}, \qquad \delta_{i\ell}(H) = I\{T_i \le \min(D_i,H,t_\ell-E_i)\}.

The success data set uses H=H_\ell; the futility data set uses H=H_F. Here, a data cut means the observations retained after restricting both calendar availability and each participant’s follow-up duration. Participants not yet enrolled contribute no observed events or exposure to either predictive model. Their predictive outcomes are generated through H_F, only for the futility assessment of success at maximum N. The implementation gives a participant enrolled exactly at the look a negligible positive exposure to accommodate the survival calculations.

For example, an event at month 15 is represented as event-free administrative censoring at month 12 in a 12-month success calculation. It can enter an 18-month futility calculation only if month 15 has already been reached at that participant’s current follow-up. A dropout at month 15 does not make the 12-month endpoint missing. A dropout at month 8 leaves the outcome after month 8 unobserved in both calculations.

Figure 1. Separate success and futility predictions. When the current and final horizons are equal, the data cuts coincide and the predictions share one fitted hazard model. When they differ, fitting one model to the longer data cut and changing only the endpoint of the completed-data analysis would allow late follow-up to inform early success; the implementation therefore fits each data cut separately.

Predictive hazard models and completed-data analyses

Gamma updating within each data cut

The analysis model has piecewise-constant hazards \lambda_{zj} for arm z and interval j, with independent shape-rate priors

\lambda_{zj} \sim \operatorname{Gamma}(a_{zj}, b_{zj}).

For a given look and horizon H, let d_{zj\ell}(H) and y_{zj\ell}(H) be the event count and total exposure in the interval after applying both the calendar and endpoint cuts. With empty_interval = "prior", the predictive posterior is

\lambda_{zj}\mid\mathcal D_\ell(H) \sim \operatorname{Gamma}\{a_{zj}+d_{zj\ell}(H),\ b_{zj}+y_{zj\ell}(H)\}.

cutpoints defines the master analysis partition. At horizon H, only cutpoints strictly less than H are retained, and the last interval ends at H. The corresponding leading columns of the interval-specific priors are retained in the same order. A cutpoint equal to H does not create an interval beyond the endpoint. Later intervals and their priors are not combined with earlier ones.

If t_1 < H < t_2, distinguish the hazard parameter from the observations used to estimate it. The master model still specifies one constant hazard on (t_1,t_2]. For success prediction at H, its likelihood uses only events and exposure in (t_1,H] that are available at the interim date. The original Gamma prior for that hazard is retained without rescaling. Thus, with prior \operatorname{Gamma}(a,b), the update is \operatorname{Gamma}\{a+d(t_1,H),b+y(t_1,H)\}. The fitted interval is displayed as (t_1,H] because the success prediction ends there; this does not introduce a new underlying hazard change at H.

For example, with cutpoints at months 6 and 15 and success endpoint 12, the second hazard is updated using observations from months 6 to 12. An observed event at month 14 supplies no event or post-12-month exposure to that success update. The separate futility model targeting month 18 can use the event and exposure through month 14 in its (6,15] interval, provided they are already observed on the look date.

An alternative would estimate the same hazard using all available observations in (t_1,t_2], then predict only through H. This borrows information beyond the success endpoint under the constant-hazard assumption and may improve precision if that assumption is appropriate. It also allows post-H observations to change success stopping. The current functions deliberately use the first approach: no observations beyond H inform success prediction, even within a shared hazard interval. Futility uses its own observations through H_F.

An interval with no observed exposure remains governed by its own prior under the default policy. This can matter substantially for the longer-horizon futility calculation at early looks. The other available policies are "propagate", the existing adjacent-interval heuristic, and "error". Bayesian piecewise-exponential designs discusses predictive and analysis priors in more detail.

Predictive completion and success scores

For each of the M= N_impute posterior draws, the success calculation imputes outstanding event times in the enrolled cohort through H_\ell. The futility calculation imputes outstanding event times among enrolled participants and generates outcomes for the remaining participants up to N_{\max}, all through H_F. Already observed events remain fixed. Imputation uses event times, including for binary analyses; independently imputed Bernoulli outcomes at different horizons are not used.

Each completed cohort is analyzed using the prespecified method. A Bayesian analysis returns the posterior probability of its alternative; a frequentist analysis returns 1-p for the specified test. Write these scores as s^{\mathrm{now}}_{\ell m} and s^{\max}_{\ell m}. For c= prob_ha, the predictive probabilities are

\widehat P_\ell = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} I(s^{\mathrm{now}}_{\ell m}>c), \qquad \widehat P_{\max,\ell} = \frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M} I(s^{\max}_{\ell m}>c).

prior_surv supplies the predictive hazard priors. For method = "bayes-surv", each completed-data analysis forms a fresh posterior using prior_surv_final and the completed cohort. It does not use the predictive posterior as a new prior, which would count the observed information twice. For method = "bayes-bin", the completed endpoint indicators are analyzed with prior_bin; the Gamma model supplies the imputation. prior_surv_final also governs hazard-based imputation at the actual final analysis when requested.

The optional horizon_settings data frame specifies horizon-specific h0, rmst_tau, or prior_bin. Without overrides, the common null value and beta prior are used at every horizon, while the RMST restriction equals the endpoint horizon. This allows, for example, different single-arm performance goals at different endpoint times. The analysis method and alternative direction remain common across horizons. The applied vignette shows how to specify different binary-risk margins at 12 and 18 months.

When success and futility use different endpoint times, they fit different observed data sets and make separate posterior and imputation draws. For example, the first completed data set for 12-month success and the first completed data set for 18-month futility are two predictive simulations, not the same simulated future followed for different durations. Their draw numbers are bookkeeping labels, not matched patient histories. The two sets estimate separate marginal predictive probabilities; they cannot be paired draw by draw to estimate a joint event. The underlying trial history used to assess the eventual trial outcomes is generated once and is shared across horizons.

Stopping and final analysis

At look \ell, the thresholds are Q_\ell= Qn, S_\ell= Sn, and F_\ell= Fn, with Q_\ell\ge S_\ell. The first applicable rule is used.

Condition Decision Endpoint and subsequent analysis
\widehat P_\ell>Q_\ell Immediate success Declare success at H_\ell without a required final analysis
S_\ell<\widehat P_\ell\le Q_\ell Expected success Stop accrual; analyze the enrolled cohort at H_\ell after endpoint ascertainment
\widehat P_\ell\le S_\ell and \widehat P_{\max,\ell}<F_\ell Binding futility Stop and classify the adaptive trial as unsuccessful
Otherwise Continue Reach the next scheduled look, or enroll to maximum N and analyze at H_F

All comparisons are strict. Qn = 1 disables immediate success, Sn = 1 disables expected-success stopping, and Fn = 0 or NULL disables futility. The Monte Carlo bounds in a trace are diagnostics and do not replace the point estimates in these comparisons.

Figure 2. The stopping sequence for a prespecified schedule. Futility is evaluated only when enabled and neither success rule applies. The diagram describes the decisions reconstructed by apply_horizon_rules() as well as direct simulation. Complete-path simulation evaluates all planned looks regardless of these hypothetical decisions.

The endpoint remains fixed after an expected-success stop, as highlighted above. The futility probability concerns the final analysis at N_{\max} and H_F; it is not the probability of declaring success at any remaining interim under the entire adaptive policy.

Final analysis with dropout follows the existing method-specific choices for imputed_final. With FALSE, survival analyses retain right-censoring, while binary analyses exclude participants without complete endpoint status. With TRUE, supported methods impute missing endpoint outcomes. Independent dropout does not by itself make complete-case binary analysis unbiased. These choices and the restrictions on log-rank and Farrington-Manning final imputation are described in the technical methods vignette.

Shared histories, dropout, and timing

Event times and dropout times are generated once per simulated trial through final_horizon. Final cohort data are re-censored at each endpoint; changing the endpoint does not redraw either process. generation_cutpoints and the arm-specific generating hazards must describe the entire collection period, and need not match the analysis partition.

If the arm-specific dropout probability is q_z by reference time H_D, then

D_i\mid Z_i=z \sim \operatorname{Exponential}(\eta_z),\qquad \eta_z=-\log(1-q_z)/H_D.

Here, H_D= dropout_horizon. This hazard remains fixed across endpoint times. With collection through H_F, the probability of dropout by that time is 1-\exp(-\eta_z H_F); the proportion actually censored by dropout can be smaller because events may occur first.

Analysis and decision dates

analysis_ready_time is the calendar date by which the event and censoring observations used in the selected endpoint’s final analysis are available. decision_time is when the trial’s success or failure is determined. Both are measured from first enrollment and exclude data-cleaning delays.

Stopping rule decision_time
Expected success The subsequent final analysis date, analysis_ready_time
Immediate success or futility The interim look date
Maximum enrollment The final analysis date, analysis_ready_time

For example, suppose recruitment stops for expected success at calendar month 30 using a 12-month endpoint. If the last participant remains event-free and observed for 12 months, both the final analysis and decision occur at month 42. A futility stop at month 30 instead determines failure immediately. Continued follow-up does not change that decision.

Reusing trial paths for calibration

How the schedule determines saved horizons

Both simulation functions take endpoint_schedule and final_horizon. Look sizes come from endpoint_schedule$N; the endpoint times to calculate are derived as sort(unique(c(endpoint_schedule$horizon, final_horizon))). The final horizon is included even if every interim uses a shorter endpoint. There is no separate interim_look or endpoint_horizons argument in these functions.

For the schedule (100,12), (200,12), (300,12), (400,18), sim_horizon_paths() evaluates current-cohort success at both 12 and 18 months at each of the four looks. It also saves maximum-cohort futility predictions at H_F=18 and final analyses for each cohort and endpoint. apply_horizon_rules() then selects one saved success endpoint per look. This permits comparison of a switch at N=300 with a switch at N=400 without new simulations. A candidate requiring an endpoint time absent from the original schedule and final horizon needs new paths.

Saving the individual completed-data scores, rather than only a predictive probability at one prob_ha, also permits recalibration of that success threshold. Reuse can change the nondecreasing success-horizon schedule within the retained looks and horizons, and Fn, Sn, Qn, and prob_ha. The generating scenario, final horizon, dropout model, analysis method, priors, horizon-specific analysis settings, maximum sample size, look sizes, and Monte Carlo counts remain fixed.

Direct simulation with sim_horizon_trials() skips unreached interim calculations. With the same seed, settings, and set of derived horizons, it agrees with complete-path simulation followed by rule application. Changing only the switch point, while retaining the same endpoint times, preserves this agreement. Removing an endpoint time entirely changes the allocation of random numbers, so direct simulation and replay from the larger horizon set need not match trial by trial. Saved settings and calculation failures remain part of the path object when written with saveRDS(); previously saved paths can still be evaluated with apply_horizon_rules().

Interpreting the two futility measures

Both measures are also available for fixed-horizon designs through sim_trial_paths() and apply_stopping_rules(); they are not specific to endpoint extensions. See Calibrating stopping rules from complete trial paths.

Suppose 1,000 evaluable trials are simulated under an alternative, 200 stop for futility, and 40 of those 200 would have succeeded if forced to continue to N_{\max} and H_F. The two reported measures answer different questions:

Measure Question Example
stop_futility What fraction of all trials stop for futility? 200/1000=20\%
futility_and_success_at_max What fraction of all trials stop for futility but would succeed at maximum N and H_F? 40/1000=4\%

The second measure uses the same simulated trial history, continued despite its futility stop. Its mathematical definition is

\Pr\{\text{binding futility and final success at }N_{\max},H_F\}.

Among futility stops alone, the corresponding fraction would be 40/200=20\%. That conditional fraction is not what futility_and_success_at_max reports.

When futility is the only early stopping rule, the 4% is exactly a 4-percentage-point loss of power. The comparison is with no early stopping (Fn = 0, Sn = Qn = 1): all 1,000 trials reach the maximum-N final analysis. Adding binding futility classifies the 40 trials that would otherwise succeed as unsuccessful. This assumes matched trial histories, analysis settings, and complete calculations. When other stopping rules are present, such as stopping for expected success, the interpretation is more complex.

Type I error across endpoint times

The design can declare success at 12 months or at 18 months. A starting null scenario is therefore one in which the treatment has no benefit at either endpoint. For example, identical control and treatment hazards throughout follow-up give identical event risks at both times. Simulate the entire procedure, including the endpoint switches and all stopping rules, and count any declaration of success. Under this scenario, that fraction is the overall type I error. Calibrating each endpoint separately does not establish control for the procedure that can stop at either one.

The null assumptions must match the hypotheses used by the chosen analysis method. For binary risk comparisons, equal risks at 18 months alone do not imply equal risks at 12 months: an early treatment benefit can disappear later. A success declared at 12 months then concerns the 12-month hypothesis; it does not establish benefit at 18 months. If the design is intended to support endpoint-specific claims with strong familywise error control, assess plausible configurations where only some endpoint null hypotheses are true as well. In those configurations, count success at a truly null endpoint, not every success; the overall power column also includes legitimate successes at endpoints with benefit. The applied example uses 12-month risks of 22% versus 30%, but an identical 18-month risk of 40.5%, and reports successes separately by endpoint. The distinction between errors at individual endpoints and overall error is discussed in FDA (2022, Sections II.B-C).

For a Cox analysis under a correctly specified proportional-hazards model, with the same null margin at every look, the treatment hazard ratio is common across follow-up horizons. Extending from 12 to 18 months then changes the available information, rather than the underlying hazard ratio. In this setting, the differing endpoint nulls illustrated by the binary-risk example are less of a concern. Multiple opportunities to stop for success still require assessment of the full stopping procedure.

Without proportional hazards, this simplification does not apply. A single Cox hazard ratio summarizes effects over the included follow-up, so extending the horizon can change the effect being summarized (Hernán, 2010). The log-rank test compares event-time distributions over the included period, not just the event risks at its endpoint. Equal risks at month 18 therefore do not establish its null hypothesis when the earlier survival curves differ; early benefit and later harm can also offset one another in the test. Switching to log-rank or Cox analysis does not, by itself, remove the need to specify the relevant null scenario.
